title: The effect of aging on skeletal-muscle recovery from exercise: possible implications for aging athletes
journal: Journal of Aging and Physical Activity
population: Review of studies of skeletal-muscle damage and recovery in older vs younger participants
findings: There is a perception among older athletes that aging negatively affects recovery; plausible arguments are a greater susceptibility of older muscle to exercise-induced damage and a slower repair and adaptation response.
Differences in physical activity level of participants are rarely considered, so the roles of declining activity and aging in recovery are hard to separate.
The exercise used to induce damage and monitor recovery is often not indicative of a normal athletic training stimulus, limiting applicability to older athletes.
The authors recommend future work use a normal training stimulus and account for participants' physical activity level.
limitations: Abstract reports no quantitative recovery-time estimate and no verdict that recovery is or is not slower; it presents the evidence as limited by design problems. Narrative review.
implications: This paper alone does not justify a change in default recovery spacing: it does not demonstrate an age-specific recovery delay in trained people.
Treat age-related recovery slowing as an individual, data-driven adjustment (readiness signals, reported soreness, session-to-session performance) rather than a fixed age multiplier.

verification.notes: Crossref match. Abstract confirms all findings; the researcher's 'inconclusive' wording is an interpretation, reworded as 'limited by design problems'.
